title: Stop Running chmod 777 in Dockerfiles: Least-Privilege Linux Permissions & BuildKit --chmod Cheatsheet
summary:
Whenever a containerized app throws EACCES: permission denied in CI or Kubernetes, the fastest "fix" people reach for is:

RUN chmod -R 777 /app

It makes the error disappear—and immediately breaks CIS Docker Benchmark hardening, lets any compromised subprocess overwrite your application binaries, and doubles your container image size because Docker creates a full copy-on-write layer for every chmod-touched file!

Here is the clean, production-safe way to handle Linux & Docker file permissions in 2026, plus an interactive 100% browser-local Chmod & Dockerfile Permission Calculator I built.

1. The 5 Production Modes You Actually Need

Octal Symbolic Use Case
400 -r-------- Read-only TLS private keys & immutable secrets
600 -rw------- SSH private keys (~/.ssh/id_ed25519) and local .env files
644 -rw-r--r-- Non-executable static assets, Nginx configs, source files
750 -rwxr-x--- Private team scripts & internal service directories
755 -rwxr-xr-x Entrypoint shell scripts and standard executables/directories

Never ship 666 or 777 (world-writable). If a container runs with readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in Kubernetes, mount a dedicated emptyDir volume only for /tmp or cache directories.

2. Use BuildKit COPY --chown --chmod Instead of RUN chmod -R

In legacy Dockerfiles, COPY . /app followed by RUN chown -R + RUN chmod -R duplicates the entire /app directory into a second image layer.

With modern Docker BuildKit, set ownership and permissions atomically during COPY:

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime

RUN addgroup --gid 10001 appgroup \
 && adduser --uid 10001 --gid 10001 --disabled-password --gecos "" appuser

WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=10001:10001 --chmod=644 ./src /app/src
COPY --chown=10001:10001 --chmod=755 ./entrypoint.sh /app/entrypoint.sh

USER 10001:10001
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/entrypoint.sh"]

Zero extra layer bloat, zero root runtime, and exact least-privilege permissions on every file.

title: When the AI Gets It Wrong in Public: Incident Response for AI Products
summary:
Every organisation that runs AI in front of customers will eventually have the same morning. A screenshot is circulating. The system said something wrong, unfair, or simply strange, and someone outside the company noticed before anyone inside it did. Support is fielding questions, a senior leader wants to know what happened, and the team that built the feature is trying to work out whether this is one bad answer or the visible tip of something larger.

Most companies have mature incident processes for outages. Very few have adapted them for AI. That gap matters, because AI incidents behave differently from traditional ones. The system is usually still up. Nothing has crashed. The logs look normal. The failure is in the quality of the output, and quality failures are harder to detect, harder to scope, and harder to explain than a server going down.

Here is how I think about building incident response for AI products, so that the bad morning is shorter, calmer, and leaves the product better than it was.

AI incidents do not look like outages

A traditional incident has a clear signal. Error rates spike, latency climbs, a health check fails, and an alert fires. The question is how fast you can restore service.

An AI incident rarely announces itself that way. The service is responding normally. Response times are fine. What has changed is that some fraction of answers are wrong, inappropriate, or harmful, and the system has no way of knowing that on its own. Often the first signal is a customer complaint, a social media post, or a frontline colleague who noticed a pattern.

That has three consequences. First, detection depends on watching quality, not just availability, which most monitoring was never designed to do. Second, the blast radius is hard to measure, because you need to know how many other users received similar answers, and that requires going back through outputs rather than counting errors. Third, the fix is rarely a restart. It may involve changing prompts, grounding data, guardrails, or the model itself, each of which needs testing before it goes live.

The first step is simply to name AI quality failures as incidents. If your incident policy only recognises downtime, a harmful answer that reaches thousands of users will be treated as a product bug and queued behind the roadmap. Define severity levels that include quality, safety, and fairness failures, with clear examples of each, so nobody has to argue at 7am about whether this counts.

Detect it before your customers do

The best incident is the one you catch internally. For AI, that means building quality signals that run continuously in production, not only at launch.

Useful signals include sampled human review of live outputs, automated checks against known failure patterns, user feedback such as thumbs down or rephrased questions, escalation rates to human agents, and sudden shifts in the distribution of answers, such as a category of response that used to be rare becoming common. None of these is perfect on its own. Together they give you a reasonable chance of noticing a problem while it is still small.

Each signal needs an owner and a threshold. A dashboard that nobody watches is not detection. Decide in advance which movements trigger a review and who gets paged, the same way you would for latency or error rates.

It also helps to make it easy for colleagues to report odd behaviour. Frontline teams see the product all day. A simple route for them to flag a suspicious answer, with the conversation attached, will surface issues faster than most automated monitoring.

Contain first, diagnose second

When an AI incident is confirmed, the instinct of most engineering teams is to find the root cause. That instinct is right eventually, but wrong as the first move. The first job is to stop further harm.

That requires containment options that exist before the incident, not ones improvised during it. The most useful are a kill switch that disables the AI feature and falls back to a safe default, a way to restrict the feature to lower-risk use cases or user groups, the ability to roll back to the previous prompt, configuration, or model version quickly, and targeted blocks for specific topics or request types while the team investigates.

Each option should be tested regularly, and the decision rights should be clear. Someone on call needs the authority to switch a feature off without convening a meeting. The cost of a feature being unavailable for a few hours is almost always smaller than the cost of it continuing to produce harmful output while people debate.

The fallback matters as much as the switch. If turning off the AI leaves users with a dead end, people will hesitate to use it. If it routes them to a simpler flow, a search result, or a human, the decision becomes easy.

Scope the damage with evidence, not hope

Once the bleeding has stopped, the next question from leadership will be how big this is. Too many teams answer with a guess, usually an optimistic one, and then have to revise it publicly.

Answering properly depends on logging decisions made long before the incident. You need to be able to retrieve the inputs, outputs, model version, configuration, and grounding sources for any given interaction, within the limits of your privacy commitments. With that record, the team can search for similar cases, estimate how many users were affected, and identify whether the problem was confined to one segment, one language, one topic, or one time window.

Without that record, the scope is unknowable, and the organisation is left choosing between overstating the problem and hoping it was small. Neither is a good position with customers, regulators, or the board.

A practical rule is that scoping should produce a number with a stated confidence and method. "We reviewed all 14,000 conversations in the affected window, found 212 with the faulty pattern, and confirmed 38 reached a user before containment" is a statement a leader can stand behind. "We think it was a handful" is not.

Communicate like you understand the system

AI incidents attract more attention than ordinary bugs, because people find machine errors unsettling in a way they do not find a slow web page unsettling. Communication therefore deserves real care.

Internally, give leadership and frontline teams a short, factual summary early, even before the full picture is clear: what happened, what has been done to contain it, what is still unknown, and when the next update will come. Update on that schedule whether or not there is news.

Externally, affected users deserve a clear account in plain language. Avoid language that blames the technology as if it were an independent actor. The organisation chose to deploy the system and is responsible for what it does. Say what went wrong, who was affected, what you have done, and what you are changing. Where individuals received harmful or incorrect information that could affect them, contact them directly and offer a route to a human who can help.

Frontline teams need their own briefing too. They are the ones customers will ask, and a short note on what to say, what not to speculate about, and where to escalate keeps the message consistent.

Prepare the templates and approval paths in advance. The middle of an incident is a poor time to discover that every external statement needs sign-off from four functions that have never discussed AI.

Run post-mortems that change the system

The post-mortem is where an incident either becomes a lasting improvement or a forgotten bad week. The standard principles still apply: blameless, focused on systems rather than individuals, and written down. AI adds some questions that traditional reviews tend to miss.

Why did our evaluation not catch this? Every AI incident is, in part, a gap in the test set. The most valuable output of the review is often a set of new evaluation cases built from the real failure, so the same problem cannot return unnoticed.

What changed? Many AI incidents follow a change nobody treated as a release: an upstream model update, a shift in source data, a new user group, a configuration tweak. Identifying the trigger shapes how future changes are tested.

Why did detection take as long as it did? If customers noticed first, the review should produce at least one new production signal.

Did containment work as designed? If the kill switch was slow, unclear, or politically difficult to use, fix that before the next incident.

Each review should end with a short list of owned actions with dates, and those actions should be tracked to completion. A post-mortem that produces insight but no change is a ritual, not a control.

Rehearse before you need it

Incident response is a skill, and skills decay without practice. The organisations that handle AI incidents well have usually rehearsed them.

A simple tabletop exercise works: take a plausible scenario, such as the assistant giving confidently wrong guidance on a sensitive topic to a few hundred users over a weekend, and walk the relevant people through it. Who notices? Who decides to switch the feature off? How do we find affected users? Who writes the customer message, and who approves it? Where are the logs we need, and can we actually query them?

These exercises reliably expose gaps that are cheap to fix in advance and expensive to discover live: missing logging, unclear authority, untested fallbacks, approval chains that take a day. An hour of rehearsal per quarter for each significant AI product is a small cost against the alternative.

The goal is not to prevent every AI incident. That is not realistic for systems that operate in an open and changing world. The goal is to make incidents smaller, shorter, and more instructive, so that every failure leaves the product measurably more reliable than before. Organisations that build that muscle earn something valuable: the confidence to keep deploying AI where it matters, because they know they can handle it when it goes wrong.

title: How to hide PHP warnings and deprecation notices on a live WordPress site
summary:
PHP warnings and notices are printing on your live WordPress pages. Set WP_DEBUG to false in wp-config.php to stop them, or pair WP_DEBUG_LOG with WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY set to false.

Why PHP warnings and notices show on live pages

Enabling WP_DEBUG causes all PHP errors, notices, and warnings to be displayed. You can turn off WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY independently to hide errors from your page HTML.

PHP's display_errors directive also determines whether errors print to the screen in output or stay hidden from users. PHP warns that display_errors is for development and should never be used on production systems connected to the internet.

Instead of displaying errors on production websites, PHP strongly advises using error logging. Pairing error logging with hidden display lets you review errors later without printing them to visitors.

Turn off debug mode in wp-config.php

Before making changes to your site, make a backup or use a staging environment first. WordPress does not recommend using WP_DEBUG or other debug tools on live sites, as they are meant for local testing and staging installs.

Open wp-config.php and find or insert the WP_DEBUG line before /* That's all, stop editing! Happy blogging. */. Set it to false to disable WP_DEBUG.

define( 'WP_DEBUG', false );

Leave false unquoted. This one is easy to miss: if you write 'false' in quotes, PHP interprets it as true because the quotes make it a string rather than a boolean.

Log errors to a file without displaying them

You can turn off WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY independently and pair it with WP_DEBUG_LOG so errors can be reviewed later. Insert these constants before /* That's all, stop editing! Happy blogging. */ in wp-config.php.

define( 'WP_DEBUG', true );
define( 'WP_DEBUG_LOG', true );
define( 'WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY', false );
@ini_set( 'display_errors', 0 );

Setting WP_DEBUG_LOG to true turns on logging, or you can set it to a valid file path to save the log elsewhere.

Watch one catch with @ini_set( 'display_errors', 0 ); in wp-config.php. PHP notes that changing display_errors at runtime with ini_set() has no effect if the script has fatal errors, because that runtime action does not execute. PHP also warns against using display_errors on production systems and advises using error logging instead.

Find which plugins need fixes before your next PHP upgrade

To check your site's PHP version, open the WordPress Dashboard, select Tools > Site Health from the sidebar menu, and open the Info tab.

WordPress recommends PHP 8.3 or higher. WordPress 6.9 added beta support for PHP 8.5, and WordPress 7.0 dropped support for PHP 7.2 and 7.3. Each PHP release branch gets two years of active support, then two more years for critical security fixes only. After four years, the branch reaches end of life and is no longer supported, so users should upgrade as soon as possible to avoid unpatched security vulnerabilities.

If your hosting company offers a staging site, update PHP there first and test your site before updating your live site.

To check installed code without turning debug output back on, I use Bright Labs Compatibility Scanner for PHP. It is a free WordPress plugin that reads every installed plugin and theme inside WordPress in short steps—needing no exec() and no shell access—and lists each file and line that uses something removed or deprecated in PHP 8.2 to 8.5 using current PHPCompatibility rules.

You can also turn on its optional update pre-scan under Tools > Bright Labs Compatibility Scanner for PHP > Settings by enabling "Check offered updates before they install", which is off by default. It checks updates WordPress offers against your server's PHP version and displays a warning on Dashboard > Updates and the Plugins screen if it finds errors, while never stopping, delaying, or changing an update.

Keep in mind that the scanner cannot promise your site will work on a newer PHP version. Because it reads code without running it, it can miss issues in code built at runtime and flag code that never runs, so treat a clean result as a good sign and test on staging first.

Checklist after you hide PHP warnings

  • Reload your live pages and verify that no PHP errors, notices, or warnings appear in the page HTML.
  • Confirm whether WP_DEBUG is false on your live site, or temporarily pairing WP_DEBUG_LOG with WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY set to false.
  • Review your WP_DEBUG_LOG file (or the custom file path you set) later to inspect logged errors.
  • Check your PHP version under Tools > Site Health > Info in the WordPress Dashboard, and test any PHP update on a staging site before updating your live site.
  • Set WP_DEBUG back to false once you finish reviewing the log, since WordPress does not recommend using WP_DEBUG on live sites.

Frequently Asked Questions

I set WP_DEBUG to 'false' in wp-config.php, so why are notices still showing?

Check whether you put quotes around false. Quoted constants like 'false' are interpreted as true because the quotes make them strings rather than booleans. Write define( 'WP_DEBUG', false ); without quotes, and make sure display_errors is not enabled on your production site.

Does setting display_errors with ini_set() in wp-config.php hide fatal errors too?

No. PHP notes that changing display_errors at runtime with ini_set() has no effect if the script has fatal errors, because the runtime action does not execute. PHP warns against using display_errors on production systems and advises using error logging instead.

Does a clean scan in Bright Labs Compatibility Scanner for PHP mean my site is ready to upgrade PHP?

The scanner cannot promise that on its own. It reads code without running it, so it can miss problems in code built at runtime and flag code that never runs. Treat a clean result as a good sign, and if your host offers a staging site, update PHP there first and test your site before updating your live site.

@ini_set( 'display_errors', 0 );

title: GitHub Actions secret is empty on pull requests: 6 causes, and why pull_request_target is the unsafe fix
summary:
Your GitHub Actions workflow works on your branch, then fails on a pull request with an empty value:

Error: Input required and not supplied: token or an API key that is just blank.

Why secrets are empty

  1. The PR comes from a fork. GitHub does not pass repository secrets to workflows triggered by pull requests from forks. This is deliberate.
  2. Secret name typo. secrets.SUPABASE_KEY and secrets.SUPABASE_ANON_KEY are different. A missing secret is an empty string, not an error.
  3. Wrong scope. The secret is set on an environment, but the job does not declare environment:. Or it is set on another repo.
  4. Dependabot. Dependabot PRs use a separate secrets store.
  5. Reusable workflow. Secrets must be passed in with secrets: or secrets: inherit.
  6. Used in an if: condition. Secrets cannot be read directly there. Map to an env var first.

The unsafe fix

The tempting fix for cause 1 is to switch the trigger to pull_request_target, which does give secrets to the run. If that workflow then checks out and runs code from the PR, a stranger's pull request can run code with your secrets and a write token. This is a well known way repository secrets get stolen.

Other unsafe fixes:

  • Printing the secret with echo to see if it is set. Logs can be read, and masking is not perfect once a value is transformed.
  • Hardcoding the key in the workflow file or committing a .env.
  • Passing the secret into a build that outputs it into your public JavaScript bundle.

The safe pattern

  • Keep pull_request for untrusted code. Run tests that need no secrets.
  • Run secret-using steps only on pushes to your protected branch, or behind a required-reviewer environment.
  • Give the workflow the least permissions: set permissions: explicitly.
  • Rotate any key that was ever echoed or committed.

An outside view

It never signs in, so it checks what a visitor can see on the live site, such as secret-shaped strings in the shipped bundle, which is where a leaky build step ends up. summary:
JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) look simple—three Base64URL-encoded strings separated by dots—so teams regularly ship subtle JWT vulnerabilities straight into production.

1. Accepting alg: "none" or Algorithm Confusion (RS256 → HS256)

If your verification middleware reads the alg field directly from the incoming untrusted JWT header instead of pinning an explicit allowlist on the server, an attacker can forge tokens with alg: "none" or sign an HS256 token using your public RSA key.

Fix: Always enforce an explicit server-side allowlist (e.g., algorithms: ['RS256'] or ['EdDSA']) and reject empty signatures.

2. Shipping Access Tokens Without exp (or 90-Day TTLs)

A JWT without an exp claim—or with a 90-day expiration—cannot be revoked cleanly if leaked in browser logs, proxies, or crash dumps.

Fix: Keep access tokens short-lived (15–60 minutes) and pair them with rotating, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax refresh tokens stored in a revocable backend table or Redis.

Remember: standard JWTs (JWS) are Base64URL-encoded, NOT encrypted. Anyone with the token—browser extensions, CDN access logs, frontend error trackers—can decode the payload in one line of JavaScript.

Never embed passwords, internal API keys, SSNs, or raw billing identifiers in JWT claims.

4. Skipping iss (Issuer) and aud (Audience) Validation

In microservice architectures where multiple apps share an IdP (Auth0, Cognito, Keycloak, Supabase), omitting aud validation lets a token minted for a low-privilege internal tool replay against your billing API.

title: Disk full? Find what's eating your space with df, du and sort (Linux)
summary:
AI disclosure: this article was created with the help of AI. An AI assistant drafted the text from the lesson script, and it was reviewed before publishing. Every command was actually run in a fresh debian:13 container (GNU coreutils 9.7); all outputs below are copied from that run, not written by hand.

A step-by-step way to find what's filling a Linux disk: check the filesystem with df -h, drill down with du -sh and du --max-depth piped into sort -h, list the biggest files with find -size, empty a log safely with truncate, and solve the classic mystery where df says the disk is full but du can't find the files (a deleted file that's still open).

The problem: No space left on device. Your app stops writing, your database refuses to start, and you need to know what's filling the disk, fast.

Step 1: which filesystem is full? df -h

Start with df. It reports space per filesystem, and -h prints sizes in human units.

$ df -h /lab
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
overlay          59G   21G   36G  37% /

In a container you see the overlay filesystem. On a server you'd look for the line with a high use percentage, usually the one mounted on slash, or on slash var. df answers which disk is full. It can't tell you which files. That's the job of du.

Step 2: which folder? du -sh

du -sh gives one total per argument. With a star, that's one line per folder here.

$ du -sh *
93M app
205M    backups
3.1M    uploads

Backups is clearly the biggest. But sorting by eye doesn't scale, so let's let the computer sort.

Step 3: drill down with --max-depth and sort -h

--max-depth=2 shows totals two levels deep, and sort -h understands human sizes, so ten megabytes sorts before one gigabyte.

$ du -h --max-depth=2 . | sort -h
3.1M    ./uploads
25M ./app/cache
69M ./app/logs
93M ./app
205M    ./backups
300M    .

The biggest are at the bottom. Plain sort, without -h, would compare the text and put a hundred megabytes before nine megabytes. To see the top offenders, files included, add -a and reverse the sort.

$ du -ah . | sort -rh | head -6
300M    .
205M    ./backups
104M    ./backups/db-2026-11.sql.gz
100M    ./backups/db-2026-10.sql.gz
93M ./app
69M ./app/logs

Step 4: list the big files with find

If you already know what's big for you, find can list every file above a size, here fifty megabytes, wherever it is.

$ find . -type f -size +50M -exec ls -lh {} +
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  60M Nov 21 19:39 ./app/logs/app.log.1
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 100M Nov 21 19:39 ./backups/db-2026-10.sql.gz
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 104M Nov 21 19:39 ./backups/db-2026-11.sql.gz

Two database dumps and a rotated log. These are the usual suspects on a real server: old backups, logs and caches.

Step 5: free space safely

To empty a log that a program may still be writing, don't delete it. truncate -s 0 cuts it to zero bytes, and the file stays in place.

$ truncate -s 0 app/logs/app.log.1 && du -sh app
33M app

Be careful with this on files you might need: the content is gone for good. For old backups, move them somewhere else before you delete anything.

The mystery: df says full, du disagrees

One more case that confuses everyone. Let's create a big temporary file.

$ fallocate -l 200M big.tmp && du -sh .
440M    .

Now a process opens it and keeps it open. Here that's just sleep, reading from the file in the background.

$ sleep 600 < big.tmp &

And someone deletes the file to free space.

$ rm big.tmp && du -sh .
240M    .

The file is gone from the folder, so du doesn't count it. But the process still holds it open, so the space is not freed, and df still shows it as used. To find such files, look for open file handles marked deleted in slash proc.

$ find /proc/*/fd -lname '*(deleted)' -printf '%p -> %l\n' 2>/dev/null
/proc/120/fd/0 -> /lab/srv/big.tmp (deleted)

The number in the path is the process I D. Stopping or restarting that process releases the space.

$ kill %1

The trap, in one paragraph

I deleted a 200 MB file, but df still counts the space as used. What is the likely cause? The space comes back only when that process closes the file, or is restarted.

Quick check

1. After du -h, why sort -h and not plain sort?

  • sort -h is faster
  • sort -h understands sizes like 9M and 100M

title: Node fetch proxy: ProxyAgent, env vars, SOCKS5 and auth
summary:
Originally published on proxymint.

Send Node's built-in fetch through a proxy: undici ProxyAgent, NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY, encoded auth, SOCKS5, rotation and the errors each mistake throws.

TL;DR

  • Pass a ProxyAgent as the dispatcher. fetch(url, { dispatcher: new ProxyAgent("http://USERNAME:PASSWORD@HOST:PORT") }) routes HTTP and HTTPS through the proxy. Import fetch and ProxyAgent from the same undici package.
  • Built-in fetch ignores HTTP_PROXY by default. Node reads the proxy variables only with NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 or --use-env-proxy, available from Node 24.0.0 and 22.21.0.
  • The undici versions must match. An npm undici 8 ProxyAgent passed to the built-in fetch on Node 22 or 24 fails with invalid onRequestStart method; on Node 22, importing undici 8 also switches the environment proxy off without an error.
  • Encode credentials or pass a token. A raw / or # in the password makes the ProxyAgent constructor throw invalid url; encodeURIComponent each part or use the token option.
  • Use undici 7.28.0 or 8.2.0 and later for SOCKS5. Socks5ProxyAgent arrived in 7.23.0, but releases before the fix can send a request to the wrong origin (CVE-2026-6734). It takes socks5:// URLs, sends host names to the proxy, and is marked experimental.

Key takeaways

  • Check process.versions.undici before copying ProxyAgent code. Keep the agent and fetch from one implementation, call install(), or pin the undici major your Node bundles.
  • Walk err.cause to read proxy failures. fetch wraps them in TypeError: fetch failed, and a refused tunnel shows its 407 two causes deep.
  • Scrub proxy URLs from logs. Node's ERR_PROXY_TUNNEL message prints the configured proxy URL with the password.
  • Test rotation with reused and fresh agents. An agent reuses tunnels per origin, and each concurrent HTTPS request opens its own CONNECT.
  • Set a timeout on every proxied call. Fetch has no overall timeout; pass AbortSignal.timeout() and retry 429, 5xx and timeouts, never 407 or 403.

Read the full guide on proxymint, with the commands, tables and sources.

title: 🔐 DNS over HTTPS (DoH): Making Internet Browsing More Private and Secure
summary:
Every time we visit a website, something happens behind the scenes before the page even loads.

Our devices need to translate domain names like google.com into IP addresses. This process is handled by DNS (Domain Name System).

But here's an interesting question:

Is traditional DNS actually private?

The answer is not entirely.

Let's explore how DNS over HTTPS (DoH) is changing the way DNS queries travel across the internet.

🌐 What Is DNS?

DNS stands for Domain Name System.

Think of it as the phonebook of the internet. It translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses that computers use to communicate.

For example:

text

google.com → 142.250.x.x

Without DNS, we would need to remember IP addresses instead of website names.

⚠️ The Problem With Traditional DNS

Traditional DNS queries usually travel over UDP port 53 without encryption.

This creates several privacy and security concerns:

  • DNS queries can potentially be observed by network intermediaries.
  • Attackers may attempt DNS spoofing or manipulation.
  • Public Wi-Fi networks can expose DNS traffic.
  • Users have limited privacy when browsing the internet.

This is where DNS over HTTPS comes in.

🔒 What Is DNS over HTTPS (DoH)?

DNS over HTTPS encrypts DNS queries by sending them through HTTPS connections.

Instead of sending traditional DNS requests over port 53, DoH sends DNS messages through HTTPS, commonly using TCP port 443.

This makes DNS queries harder for network intermediaries to inspect or modify.

⚡ How Does DoH Work?

Here's a simplified process:

  1. A user enters a website address in a browser.
  2. The browser creates a DNS query.
  3. The DNS query is encrypted and sent over HTTPS.
  4. A DoH resolver receives and processes the request.
  5. The resolver returns the IP address through the encrypted connection.
  6. The browser connects to the destination website.

🔍 Traditional DNS vs DNS over HTTPS

Feature Traditional DNS DNS over HTTPS
Default Port UDP/TCP 53 TCP 443
Encryption Usually none HTTPS encryption
Privacy Limited Improved
Transport DNS protocol DNS over HTTPS
Visibility Easier to inspect Harder to inspect

🛠️ Why Should Network Engineers Care?

DoH introduces important changes for network administrators and security professionals.

1. Network Monitoring

Traditional DNS monitoring becomes more difficult when DNS queries are encrypted.

2. Firewall Management

Organizations may need updated security policies to manage encrypted DNS traffic.

3. Security Visibility

Security teams need alternative approaches to identify suspicious DNS activity.

4. Privacy Protection

DoH helps protect DNS queries from passive observation on the network.

5. Enterprise Networks

Organizations should establish policies for approved DNS resolvers and encrypted DNS services.

🧪 Can You Try It?

Modern browsers such as Firefox and Chrome support DNS over HTTPS.

You can explore the feature through browser security and privacy settings.

You can also learn about public DoH resolver services and experiment in a controlled environment.

🚀 Final Thoughts

DNS is one of the most important components of internet infrastructure, but it has traditionally lacked encryption.

DNS over HTTPS represents an important step toward improving DNS privacy.

However, encryption does not automatically mean complete anonymity. Your DNS resolver can still see your queries, and other network activity may reveal information about your browsing.

As networking professionals, understanding technologies like DoH is essential as internet infrastructure continues to evolve.

💬 Let's Discuss!

I'd love to hear your thoughts:

  • Do you use DNS over HTTPS in your browser?
  • Should organizations allow employees to use public DoH resolvers?
  • Does encrypted DNS improve security, or does it make network monitoring more difficult?

Share your experience in the comments!

title: Fix Ollama CPU offload when the GPU model runs slow
summary:
Originally published on kuryzhev.cloud

Failure scenario: the GPU is "in use" but the model crawls

A typical case of Ollama CPU offload goes like this. A developer has a 16 GB GPU and a mid-sized quantized model that answered quickly all week. Then they point a coding agent or IDE plugin at it and raise the context window to 32k so it can read more files. Generation drops from fluent to a token every few hundred milliseconds. Nothing errors, and the model still answers, only slowly.

nvidia-smi shows VRAM nearly full, so everything looks fine. But GPU utilization is low and a few CPU cores are pinned. Part of the model is running on the CPU, and Ollama did not announce it.

Short answer: run ollama ps and read the PROCESSOR column. If it says anything other than 100% GPU, the model plus its context cache no longer fits in VRAM. Lower num_ctx, quantize the KV cache, cut parallel slots, or pick a smaller model or quant until it reads 100% GPU again. This applies whenever a model that used to be fast slows down after a context, model or tooling change.

The symptom is easy to misdiagnose because nothing breaks. The server stays up, the API returns 200s, and quality is unchanged. Only latency gets worse. CPU-bound token generation can be several times slower than a fully GPU-resident run, and the exact ratio depends on your hardware.

Why it happens: weights are not the only thing in VRAM

Ollama loads model weights into VRAM, and it also allocates a KV cache for the context window. That cache grows linearly with context length, so doubling num_ctx roughly doubles it. A model whose weights fit with room to spare at a small context can overflow once the context is raised.

When the total does not fit, Ollama does not refuse to load. It splits the model by layers and keeps what fits on the GPU. The rest runs on the CPU from system RAM. Every token then crosses that boundary, and the slow CPU layers set the pace for the whole pass. This is the documented fallback behavior. It is also why a 10% spill can feel much worse than 10% slower.

Several things inflate memory without you touching the model:

  • Client-side context overrides. Many tools send options.num_ctx per request, overriding whatever you set in a Modelfile or on the server. Check what the client actually sends.
  • Parallel slots. OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL multiplies the context memory, because each slot needs its own share.
  • A second loaded model. Models stay resident for the keep-alive period (five minutes by default). A chat model and an embedding model can share the card and push each other into offload.
  • Default context changes. Recent Ollama releases may choose a default context based on available VRAM. This is version-dependent, so verify against the official Ollama docs for your installed version.
  • No GPU at all. A container started without --gpus=all, or a driver that stopped loading after a kernel update, means 100% CPU. ollama ps shows that too.

Watch out for: nvidia-smi alone will not tell you this. Full VRAM is normal in both the healthy and the offloaded case. The split lives in Ollama's own view.

The fix: size the context to the card, then verify

First, confirm the diagnosis. Load the model the way your tool does by sending a real request, then check:

# Which processor is each loaded model on?
ollama ps
# Expected shape when healthy:
#   NAME   ID   SIZE   PROCESSOR   CONTEXT   UNTIL
#   ...                100% GPU    ...
# Offloaded shape: a split like "NN%/MM% CPU/GPU" in PROCESSOR

# Watch VRAM while you test
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total --format=csv -l 2

# On a systemd install, the server log reports how many layers went to the GPU
journalctl -u ollama --since "10 min ago" | grep -i -E "offload|layers"

If the processor column shows a split, apply server-level settings. On Linux with systemd, run sudo systemctl edit ollama and add an override:

[Service]
# Default context for every model; a Modelfile or a per-request num_ctx overrides it
Environment="OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=8192"
# Flash attention is required for KV cache quantization
Environment="OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1"
# Roughly halves KV cache memory versus f16; small quality cost
Environment="OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0"
# One slot unless you really serve concurrent users
Environment="OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1"
# Do not keep idle models fighting for VRAM
Environment="OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=1"

Then run sudo systemctl restart ollama. If you run the Ollama container, pass the same variables with -e flags. You must recreate the container for new values to take effect.

For a model you use constantly, pin its default context in a Modelfile. Tools that send their own num_ctx will still override it, so audit those clients too:

cat > Modelfile <<'EOF'
FROM your-model:tag
PARAMETER num_ctx 8192
EOF
ollama create your-model-8k -f Modelfile
ollama stop your-model:tag    # unload the old instance
ollama run your-model-8k "hello" && ollama ps

Verify it worked: ollama ps should now report 100% GPU, and the CONTEXT column should show the value you set. Run ollama run --verbose your-model-8k and compare the reported eval rate before and after. Use your own numbers, since they vary by card and model.

What this costs: a smaller context means agents see less of your repository per request, and long prompts get truncated. Quantizing the KV cache saves memory but can slightly degrade output on long contexts, and q4_0 is more aggressive than q8_0. If you truly need a 32k+ window, shaving settings will not get you there. The honest fix is a smaller model, a lower weight quantization, or a card with more VRAM. Partial offload can still be acceptable for batch jobs where latency does not matter.

Watch out for: server environment variables are read only when the server starts. Restart the service (or recreate the container) after changing them, which also unloads models. Modelfile changes need the model unloaded with ollama stop and reloaded. Otherwise you are testing the old allocation.

Prevention checklist

Offload is easiest to catch before it reaches users. Make the processor split a visible check, not something you discover through complaints. The block below can live in a team README or a pre-flight script:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# preflight-ollama.sh: fail if any loaded model is not fully on GPU
set -euo pipefail
out=$(ollama ps | tail -n +2)
[ -z "$out" ] && { echo "no model loaded; send a request first"; exit 2; }
if grep -q "CPU" <<<"$out"; then
  echo "CPU offload detected:"; echo "$out"; exit 1
fi
echo "all loaded models are 100% GPU"

# Keepable alias:
# alias ops='watch -n2 ollama ps'

The checklist to adopt:

  • Record the VRAM budget for each shared GPU: weights, KV cache at your chosen context, and headroom for a second model.
  • Set OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH explicitly on the server instead of relying on a default that may change between releases.
  • Pin num_ctx in Modelfiles for models you depend on, and audit what your IDE and agent tools send per request.
  • Keep OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL at 1 on small cards. Raise it only after measuring.
  • Re-run ollama ps after every model pull, context change, driver update or kernel update.
  • In containers, confirm GPU access once with nvidia-smi inside the container and again with ollama ps.
  • Treat a sudden tokens-per-second drop as a capacity signal. Check for CPU in the processor column before blaming the model.

When this approach is not enough: if several people share one GPU, tuning flags only delays the problem. You need a scheduling layer or dedicated cards per workload. On Kubernetes, that means requesting GPUs explicitly rather than hoping a single node's card is free. You can do this through the device plugin's nvidia.com/gpu resource or, since Kubernetes v1.37, DRA-backed extended resources, which are now GA.

Flag names and defaults move between Ollama releases, so cross-check this article against the Ollama documentation for your installed version. For more practical notes on running AI tooling in production, see kuryzhev.cloud.

# Which processor is each loaded model on?

# Expected shape when healthy:
#   NAME   ID   SIZE   PROCESSOR   CONTEXT   UNTIL
#   ...                100% GPU    ...
# Offloaded shape: a split like "NN%/MM% CPU/GPU" in PROCESSOR

If the processor column shows a split, apply server-level settings. On Linux with systemd, run sudo systemctl edit ollama and add an override:

# Flash attention is required for KV cache quantization

# Roughly halves KV cache memory versus f16; small quality cost

# One slot unless you really serve concurrent users

# Do not keep idle models fighting for VRAM

Then run sudo systemctl restart ollama. If you run the Ollama container, pass the same variables with -e flags. You must recreate the container for new values to take effect.

EOF

Offload is easiest to catch before it reaches users. Make the processor split a visible check, not something you discover through complaints. The block below can live in a team README or a pre-flight script:

  • In containers, confirm GPU access once with nvidia-smi inside the container and again with ollama ps.
  • Treat a sudden tokens-per-second drop as a capacity signal. Check for CPU in the processor column before blaming the model.

When this approach is not enough: if several people share one GPU, tuning flags only delays the problem. You need a scheduling layer or dedicated cards per workload. title: "Closed for maintenance" is an architecture choice
summary:
You probably can't remember the last time WhatsApp or Facebook told you it was closed for an update. How they deploy internally I don't know. What I do know is the general technique for any service that runs on many servers: update a few at a time while the rest keep serving, then move on to the next few. Nobody is switched over all at once, and nobody notices.

Many older systems were built differently. A system designed around a nightly batch often has to stop writes while the batch runs, because the batch needs a consistent view of the day and locking everything is the simplest way to get one. "Closed for maintenance" is the visible result of that design. It is not a law of nature.

If you are designing something today, ask for zero-downtime updates from day one. Retrofitting them into a system that assumes a quiet night is far harder than building them in. Below are the seven things I would check, with the failure modes that make each one more than a checkbox.

One idea runs through all of them. During a rolling deploy, version N and version N+1 run side by side, and they share everything: the database, the cache, the queues and the API clients. Every shared thing has to work with both versions, in both directions.

Roll out gradually, and let health checks decide

Rolling, blue-green and canary deployments differ in how much of the fleet changes at once, but all of them need a gate that stops the rollout when something is wrong. Here is a Kubernetes-flavoured config. The same ideas exist in other orchestrators.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 6
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1          # start one new instance before stopping an old one
      maxUnavailable: 0    # never drop below the desired replica count
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: api }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: api }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45   # covers preStop plus shutdown
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/api:2026-11-19
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 2
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec: { command: ["sleep", "10"] }   # needs a sleep binary in the image

With maxUnavailable: 0, an instance that never becomes ready stalls the rollout and the old instances keep serving. That is the behavior you want.

The probe is where teams go wrong. A readiness check that only returns 200 proves the process is up, not that the new version works. Gate on the things users feel: error rate and latency of the new instances compared with the old ones, after a bake period long enough to see them. Keep readiness separate from liveness. If a liveness probe depends on the database, a database blip restarts every instance at once, which turns a slow dependency into a full outage.

Blue-green gives you an instant switch at the cost of roughly double capacity during the rollout. Canary sends a small share of traffic first and is only as good as the metrics you compare.

Drain connections before removing an instance

When an instance is told to stop, requests are in flight. If it exits immediately, they fail. The order should be:

  1. Stop receiving new traffic: fail the readiness check.
  2. Wait for the load balancer to notice. Endpoint removal propagates asynchronously, which is the reason for the preStop pause in the config above.
  3. Stop accepting new connections and let in-flight requests finish, up to a deadline.
  4. Exit before the grace period ends, or the orchestrator kills the process anyway.

Long-lived connections need extra care. A WebSocket does not finish on its own, so the server has to close it and the client has to reconnect. If every client reconnects at the same moment, the new instances take a burst they were not sized for. Reconnect with a random delay, and close connections gradually rather than all at once.

Make database changes backward compatible

This is the part that most often forces downtime. Renaming or replacing a column in one release means that during the rollout, half the fleet runs code that does not understand the schema. The pattern that avoids it is expand, migrate, contract, spread over separate releases:

-- Release 1 (expand): additive only, so nothing running today can break.
SET lock_timeout = '3s';          -- fail fast instead of queueing behind a long transaction
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN phone_e164 text;

-- Release 2 ships code that writes both columns and reads phone_e164,
-- falling back to phone when it is NULL.

-- Backfill in small batches, repeated until it updates 0 rows.
-- normalize_phone() is a stand-in for your own function.
UPDATE customers
SET    phone_e164 = normalize_phone(phone)
WHERE  id IN (
    SELECT id FROM customers
    WHERE  phone_e164 IS NULL AND phone IS NOT NULL
    ORDER  BY id
    LIMIT  1000
);

-- Release 3 stops reading and writing phone.

-- Release 4 (contract): only now remove the old column.
ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN phone;

The reason for the wait between steps is rollback. Until release 4, any earlier release can be redeployed and still works. If the column had been dropped in the same release as the code that stops using it, rolling back the code would break against the new schema.

Some PostgreSQL specifics worth knowing. An ALTER TABLE needs a strong lock. If a long-running transaction holds a conflicting lock, the ALTER waits, and every query that arrives after it queues behind it, so a harmless-looking migration becomes an outage. That is why lock_timeout is set above: fail, then retry. Adding a column with a constant default is fast since PostgreSQL 11 because it only touches the catalog; a volatile default such as clock_timestamp() still rewrites the table. Adding a constraint to a large table is safer as ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID followed by VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, and indexes should be built with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

The cost is real: a rename becomes four releases. I accept that for tables that serve live traffic. For a table nobody reads during the day, a single release is fine.

Version your APIs and keep old mobile clients working

On the web you control what the user runs. On mobile you do not. People stay on old versions for weeks or months, so every server release has to work with every client version you still support. Mobile releases also pass through store review, which means a fix to a broken old client is not instant.

The server side of that is mostly discipline: add fields, never remove or repurpose them, and make new behavior opt-in. The client side is a tolerant reader. A client written before a new enum value existed must not crash when the server sends it:

enum OrderStatus {
  pending, shipped, delivered, unknown;

  static OrderStatus parse(String? raw) => OrderStatus.values.firstWhere(
        (s) => s.name == raw,
        orElse: () => OrderStatus.unknown,
      );
}

The UI then shows something neutral for unknown instead of throwing. Ship that behavior in the first version of the app, because it only protects clients that already contain it.

Have the app send its version in a header, and log which versions still call which endpoints. That data tells you when an old endpoint can be retired. A forced-update screen is the last resort, not the plan.

Decouple "end of day" from availability

Day-close, reconciliation and reports do not need a lock on the whole system. They need a consistent view of a point in time, and databases can provide that without stopping anyone. In PostgreSQL, a repeatable-read transaction sees one snapshot for its whole life:

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY;
SELECT sum(amount) FROM ledger_entries WHERE business_date = DATE '2026-11-18';
-- every further query in this transaction sees the same snapshot
COMMIT;

The second half of the design is in the data model. Stamp each entry with a business_date. Closing a day becomes a state change on that date, and anything posted afterwards goes to the next day or to a clearly marked adjustment that references the closed one. The system keeps taking writes the whole time.

Run heavy reports on a read replica. A long transaction on the primary holds back cleanup of old row versions, and on a busy table that cost shows up.

Use feature flags so deploy and enable are separate decisions

When shipping code and turning on behavior are one event, every deploy is a release. A flag splits them: deploy dark, enable for a small group, widen, and switch it off in seconds if it misbehaves, without a rollback.

Flags have failure modes of their own. Decide what the code does when the flag service is unreachable, and keep sensible defaults compiled into the app, since mobile clients cannot wait for a network call. Remove flags once a rollout is finished, because a codebase full of stale flags has more states than anyone can test. Flags also pair with expand-contract: flipping the read path from phone to phone_e164 becomes a flag, not a deploy.

Keep a rollback path you have rehearsed

A rollback you have never run is a hope. It also has more parts than "deploy the previous version": the previous artifact must still exist, its configuration must still be valid, and the database must still work with it. The expand-contract rule above exists to keep that last part true.

Rehearse it. In staging, deploy N+1 under load, roll back to N while the load continues, and measure the time and the errors. Write down the criteria for choosing between rolling back and rolling forward, so nobody invents them at 2 a.m. Wire an automatic rollback to the same metrics that gate the rollout, so a bad canary reverts without waiting for a person.

When the answer is a maintenance window

Zero downtime has a price. It needs spare capacity during rollouts, more releases for schema changes, a test matrix of mixed versions, and flag hygiene. A small internal tool used by one office from nine to five may be better served by a short, announced window. The argument is not that every system needs this. It is that the window should be a decision someone made on purpose, because the alternative is the architecture making it for you.

title: Your CVE backlog is not a patch queue
summary:
There is a lot of talk about vulnerabilities and vulnerability scanning after the recent fiasco with the PHP and Java shell issues. Most organizations have had to undertake emergency vulnerability fixes after this discovery. On the implementation end, one highly publicized vulnerability consumes a sprint while another, with evidence of active exploitation, remains in the backlog.

The typical approach taken under these circumstances is - Patch everything immediately, because the cost of waiting may be an incident. Or stop reacting to every alert, because the team cannot turn every scanner result into an emergency change.

Neither position gives an engineering team a workable operating model.

Patching is necessary. Emergency patching is a prioritization decision. When every finding enters the same urgent queue, the queue is no longer describing risk. It is describing which advisory produced the loudest notification.

I would separate vulnerability discovery from vulnerability response.

The volume has already broken the flat queue

The pressure is not imaginary. In April 2026, NIST changed how it enriches CVEs in the National Vulnerability Database. CVE submissions had increased 263% between 2020 and 2025. NIST enriched nearly 42,000 CVEs in 2025, 45% more than in any previous year, and still concluded that processing every submission in the same way was not sustainable.

Its new workflow prioritizes known exploited vulnerabilities, software used by the US federal government, and software classified as critical. Other CVEs remain in the database but may not receive immediate enrichment.

That is an important operational signal. Even the organization maintaining the NVD had to distinguish intake from priority.

Many internal processes still do the opposite:

scanner finding
      ↓
critical severity
      ↓
urgent ticket
      ↓
interrupt the owning team

This looks decisive. It also drops most of the information required to decide what to do.

The product may not be deployed. The vulnerable component may exist in an image but never be loaded. The service may be isolated from the attack path. A compensating control may reduce exposure. Conversely, a medium-severity vulnerability on an internet-facing identity service may deserve attention before a critical issue in a disconnected test tool.

Severity is useful evidence. It is not the whole decision.

Build an exposure record, not another ticket

I would turn each finding into a small exposure record before assigning a response lane.

advisory
   ↓
product and version match
   ↓
deployed asset validation
   ↓
reachability and exposure
   ↓
exploitation evidence
   ↓
business consequence
   ↓
response lane and owner
   ↓
remediation verification

The first two checks answer whether the vulnerability could apply. The next three answer whether it matters now. Only then does a patch ticket have enough context to displace planned work.

The record does not need to become a security data platform with seventeen integrations (tempting, but unnecessary for version one). A table with the following fields is enough to expose where the process is weak:

  • CVE and affected product
  • deployed asset or workload
  • internet-facing or internal exposure
  • known exploitation status
  • exploit probability or threat signal
  • expected business impact
  • compensating control
  • service owner and patch owner
  • chosen action and due date
  • validation evidence

The asset is the join key. Without a current inventory, a scanner can tell you that a package is vulnerable but not where the deployed risk lives or who can remove it.

Use several signals, but do not pretend they are interchangeable

CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog identifies vulnerabilities with evidence of exploitation in the wild. That is stronger urgency evidence than a theoretical severity score.

EPSS answers a different question. It estimates the probability that exploitation activity will be observed for a CVE in the next 30 days, and it updates the score daily. FIRST is explicit that EPSS is not a complete risk score. It does not know whether the product exists in your environment, whether the vulnerable path is reachable, what controls you have, or what damage exploitation would cause.

CISA's Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization guide adds decision points such as exploitation status, technical impact, and the effect on a particular organization. The useful idea is not that every company must copy the federal decision tree. It is that vulnerability response should end in an action decision, not another number.

I would use the signals like this:

Signal What it contributes What it cannot decide
Severity Potential technical impact Whether your instance is exposed
CISA KEV Confirmed exploitation evidence Whether you run the affected product
EPSS Near-term exploitation probability Local consequence and controls
Asset context Presence, reachability, owner Threat activity outside the organization
Business context Consequence and acceptable downtime Whether exploitation is occurring

No single column should automatically become the priority. The combination should.

Give findings a response lane

A useful triage process produces a small number of operational outcomes. I would start with four.

Lane Typical evidence Response
Act now Known exploitation plus a reachable, consequential asset Mitigate or patch out of band; open an incident if compromise is plausible
Accelerate High exploit likelihood or serious exposure without confirmed exploitation Patch through a shortened, staged release path
Maintain Affected but contained, with no strong exploitation signal Include in the normal maintenance cycle
Track Not deployed, not reachable, or awaiting better evidence Record the reason and reassess when evidence changes

"Track" does not mean forget. Threat intelligence changes. Assets move. A package that was unreachable last week may become exposed after a routing change. The exposure record needs a review trigger, not an eternal exception.

This also avoids the opposite mistake: using risk-based prioritization as permission to leave routine patching indefinitely undone. NIST's patch-management guidance describes patching as preventive maintenance and includes identification, prioritization, installation, and verification. Prioritization decides the route and timing. It does not remove the maintenance obligation.

Separate the owners before the alert arrives

The most expensive vulnerability meeting is the one where everyone agrees the issue is urgent and nobody can say who owns the change.

I would split responsibility explicitly:

  • Security owns threat intelligence, triage policy, and the evidence required for an exception.
  • Platform teams own shared base images, cluster components, patch automation, and safe rollout mechanisms.
  • Service owners validate application compatibility and confirm whether vulnerable functionality is reachable.
  • Business or product owners accept downtime, feature displacement, or a documented deferral when the trade-off is material.

The boundaries will vary, but the handoff cannot be implicit. Security should not throw a spreadsheet over the wall. Platform engineering should not decide business consequence alone. A product owner should not be able to defer an exploited internet-facing vulnerability without a recorded decision.

For common dependencies, centralize the repair path. If ninety workloads inherit the same base image, rebuilding ninety application repositories by hand is the wrong abstraction. Publish a patched base, rebuild through a standard pipeline, deploy in cohorts, and give service owners a clear compatibility window.

event_model_payload.headline: Your CVE backlog is not a patch queue
event_model_payload.summary:
There is a lot of talk about vulnerabilities and vulnerability scanning after the recent fiasco with the PHP and Java shell issues. Most organizations have had to undertake emergency vulnerability fixes after this discovery. On the implementation end, one highly publicized vulnerability consumes a sprint while another, with evidence of active exploitation, remains in the backlog.

The typical approach taken under these circumstances is - Patch everything immediately, because the cost of waiting may be an incident. Or stop reacting to every alert, because the team cannot turn every scanner result into an emergency change.

Neither position gives an engineering team a workable operating model.

Patching is necessary. Emergency patching is a prioritization decision. When every finding enters the same urgent queue, the queue is no longer describing risk. It is describing which advisory produced the loudest notification.

I would separate vulnerability discovery from vulnerability response.

The volume has already broken the flat queue

The pressure is not imaginary. In April 2026, NIST changed how it enriches CVEs in the National Vulnerability Database. CVE submissions had increased 263% between 2020 and 2025. NIST enriched nearly 42,000 CVEs in 2025, 45% more than in any previous year, and still concluded that processing every submission in the same way was not sustainable.

Its new workflow prioritizes known exploited vulnerabilities, software used by the US federal government, and software classified as critical. Other CVEs remain in the database but may not receive immediate enrichment.

That is an important operational signal. Even the organization maintaining the NVD had to distinguish intake from priority.

Many internal processes still do the opposite:

scanner finding
      ↓
critical severity
      ↓
urgent ticket
      ↓
interrupt the owning team

This looks decisive. It also drops most of the information required to decide what to do.

The product may not be deployed. The vulnerable component may exist in an image but never be loaded. The service may be isolated from the attack path. A compensating control may reduce exposure. Conversely, a medium-severity vulnerability on an internet-facing identity service may deserve attention before a critical issue in a disconnected test tool.

Severity is useful evidence. It is not the whole decision.

I would turn each finding into a small exposure record before assigning a response lane.

advisory

product and version match
   ↓
deployed asset validation
   ↓
reachability and exposure
   ↓
exploitation evidence
   ↓
business consequence
   ↓
response lane and owner
   ↓

The first two checks answer whether the vulnerability could apply. The next three answer whether it matters now. Only then does a patch ticket have enough context to displace planned work.

The record does not need to become a security data platform with seventeen integrations (tempting, but unnecessary for version one). A table with the following fields is enough to expose where the process is weak:

  • CVE and affected product
  • deployed asset or workload
  • internet-facing or internal exposure
  • known exploitation status
  • exploit probability or threat signal
  • expected business impact
  • compensating control
  • service owner and patch owner
  • chosen action and due date
  • validation evidence

The asset is the join key. Without a current inventory, a scanner can tell you that a package is vulnerable but not where the deployed risk lives or who can remove it.

Use several signals, but do not pretend they are interchangeable

CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog identifies vulnerabilities with evidence of exploitation in the wild. That is stronger urgency evidence than a theoretical severity score.

EPSS answers a different question. It estimates the probability that exploitation activity will be observed for a CVE in the next 30 days, and it updates the score daily. FIRST is explicit that EPSS is not a complete risk score. It does not know whether the product exists in your environment, whether the vulnerable path is reachable, what controls you have, or what damage exploitation would cause.

CISA's Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization guide adds decision points such as exploitation status, technical impact, and the effect on a particular organization. CISA KEV Confirmed exploitation evidence Whether you run the affected product
EPSS Near-term exploitation probability Local consequence and controls

Business context Consequence and acceptable downtime Whether exploitation is occurring

No single column should automatically become the priority. The combination should.

Lane Typical evidence Response
Act now Known exploitation plus a reachable, consequential asset Mitigate or patch out of band; open an incident if compromise is plausible

Maintain Affected but contained, with no strong exploitation signal Include in the normal maintenance cycle
Track Not deployed, not reachable, or awaiting better evidence Record the reason and reassess when evidence changes
